  • Legitimate Budibase query builder where an admin genuinely writes a query containing the word DELETE or DROP as part of app logic
  • WAF learning/tuning mode replaying captured payloads
  • A user field legitimately containing text like 'grant all access' being URL-encoded into the request
  • Automated regression tests that exercise datasource CRUD endpoints
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("10.0.0.0/8")) // exclude sanctioned internal scanner ranges; replace with your DAST subnet
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy log and confirm the second statement after `;` is attacker-controlled (DROP/DELETE/OUTFILE/GRANT) rather than app-legitimate text; note source IP, auth state and whether it hit /api/queries/preview. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, disable the affected MySQL datasource in Budibase, and upgrade @budibase/server past 3.38.1 (or hot-patch multipleStatements:false in packages/server/src/integrations/mysql.ts). 3) Hunt: review MySQL general/audit logs for stacked statements from the Budibase DB user, and run UC-2 to check whether mysqld wrote any INTO OUTFILE dumps to /tmp or the web root.

MySQL server (mysqld) writes exfil file via SELECT INTO OUTFILE on Budibase DB host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the mysqld process creating files outside its data directory — the server-side footprint of a successful SELECT INTO OUTFILE data-theft chain that the Budibase multipleStatements SQL injection enables. Article-specific because the advisory explicitly lists 'Exfiltrate data via SELECT INTO OUTFILE' as an impact, and mysqld writing to /tmp, a web root, or Temp is anomalous for a normal DB workload. Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's named exfil primitive (SELECT INTO OUTFILE) by detecting mysqld itself creating files outside /var/lib/mysql - a behaviour that normal Budibase-driven MySQL workloads never exhibit. Excludes the datadir to keep the signal clean. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@budibase/server/GHSA-q6x4-v3qx-85qw/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/server-budibase-sql-injection-via-multiplestatements-true-3b00631cb39a1028
ATT&CKT1190 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA using SELECT INTO OUTFILE for a legitimate scheduled data export to a reporting directory
  • mysqldump or backup tooling writing dumps to /tmp or a staging path
  • MySQL error/slow-query logs configured to write outside the datadir
  • Application code that legitimately exports CSVs via the DB engine
  • Migration jobs writing .sql files during a maintenance window

| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/var/backups/", "/opt/mysql-exports/")) // exclude sanctioned DBA export/backup directories
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the created file, open it read-only to confirm it contains dumped table rows, and correlate its creation time against UC-1 WAF hits / the Budibase datasource user's MySQL query log. 2) Contain: preserve then remove the exfil file, disable the Budibase MySQL datasource, set secure_file_priv to a locked-down path (or NULL to disable OUTFILE), and revoke FILE privilege from the Budibase DB account. 3) Hunt: search web-server and proxy egress for retrieval of the written file, review MySQL logs for other stacked statements from the same session, and confirm no DROP/DELETE (data destruction) statements executed.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("mysqld.exe","mysqld")
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", "/tmp/", @"\inetpub\", "/var/www/", @"\www\") or FileName endswith ".csv" or FileName endswith ".sql" or FileName endswith ".txt"
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/mysql/", @"\MySQL\", @"\Data\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("mysqld","mysqld.exe")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/www/","\\Temp\\","\\inetpub\\") or TargetFileName endswith ".csv" or TargetFileName endswith ".sql" or TargetFileName endswith ".txt"
| where not(TargetFilePath has_any ("/var/lib/mysql/","\\Data\\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

OpenAM /authservice CustomCallback ClassName XML — CVE-2026-62379 pre-auth Class.forName RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound PLL remote-auth requests to OpenAM's /authservice endpoint whose XML body carries a <CustomCallback>/<ClassName> element — the exact vector CVE-2026-62379 abuses to make the server Class.forName-load and instantiate an attacker-named Java class without authentication. Article-specific because it keys on the two OpenAM remote-auth DTD tags that drive the vulnerable code path, not generic 'suspicious POST'. Rationale: Keys on the concrete OpenAM PLL remote-auth tokens `/authservice` + `<CustomCallback>`/`<ClassName>` that AuthXMLUtils.createCustomCallback passes to Class.forName (per the GHSA and OffSeq/GitLab write-ups); a POST to that endpoint carrying those XML tags is the exploit itself, not a generic probe. Body match requires a proxy/WAF that logs request payloads. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wg5r-wc3x-39vc • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/orgopenidentityplatformopenamopenam-core-openam-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-via-classforname-7678e3fe5efb8e5c • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/org.openidentityplatform.openam/openam-scripting/CVE-2026-47424/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured distributed-auth UI or policy agents that POST CustomCallback XML to /authservice when a site genuinely uses custom callback modules
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the endpoint post-disclosure
  • Internal red-team / patch-validation testing of CVE-2026-62379
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting /authservice (these lack the CustomCallback/ClassName body, so the body filter suppresses them)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","nikto") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request body for the matched event; inspect the <ClassName> value — a JDK/attacker-controlled class (e.g. anything not an OpenAM callback package) plus an external/unauthenticated SourceIP is a true positive. Confirm the target OpenAM build is <=16.1.1. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, enable sunRemoteAuthSecurityEnabled to force the remote-auth security token, and restrict external access to /authservice; schedule the 16.1.2 upgrade. 3) Hunt: pivot to the OpenAM host and check for java/tomcat spawning shells (UC2), new .jsp files under webapps, and outbound connections from the app-server user in the minutes following the request.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/authservice"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
// <CustomCallback>/<ClassName> are the OpenAM remote-auth DTD tags Class.forName consumes
| where Message has_any ("CustomCallback","ClassName") or RequestContext has_any ("CustomCallback","ClassName") or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("CustomCallback","ClassName") or DeviceCustomString2 has_any ("CustomCallback","ClassName")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/authservice*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/authservice*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
OpenAM/Tomcat java process spawning shell or LOLBin — CVE-2026-62379 post-exploitation AIInstallation High
Detects the OpenAM app-server JVM (java/javaw, Tomcat/Catalina) spawning an interactive shell or download/recon LOLBin — the immediate on-host consequence of CVE-2026-62379 instantiating attacker code via Class.forName. Scoped to OpenAM by requiring openam/catalina/tomcat/forgerock in the parent command line so it isn't a generic 'java spawns cmd' rule. Rationale: OpenAM is a Java/Tomcat app, so successful CVE-2026-62379 code execution surfaces as the JVM parenting a shell/LOLBin; anchoring the parent command line to openam/catalina/tomcat/forgerock keeps it OpenAM-specific and strips generic java build-tool noise. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory and OffSeq threat radar entry describing full-server code execution. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wg5r-wc3x-39vc • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/orgopenidentityplatformopenamopenam-core-openam-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-via-classforname-7678e3fe5efb8e5c
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenAM/Tomcat lifecycle scripts (catalina.sh start/stop) that legitimately fork a shell during startup or shutdown
  • ssoadm / amster CLI or backup cron jobs invoked through the app-server user that shell out
  • Monitoring/APM agents embedded in the JVM that exec helper binaries (e.g. curl for health probes)
  • Admin running diagnostic commands (whoami/net) under the tomcat service account during maintenance
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("catalina.sh start","catalina.sh stop","catalina.sh run","shutdown","ssoadm","amster")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine — recon (whoami/id/net), downloaders (curl/wget/certutil to external hosts), or reverse-shell one-liners under the tomcat/openam service account are true positives; benign catalina start/stop is not. Correlate the timestamp against UC1 /authservice hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, rotate OpenAM service-account and datastore/admin credentials, and enable sunRemoteAuthSecurityEnabled while scheduling the 16.1.2 upgrade. 3) Hunt: look for dropped .jsp/.class webshells under Tomcat webapps, new cron/systemd or scheduled-task persistence created by the service user, and outbound C2 from the JVM.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe")
// scope to the OpenAM/Tomcat JVM, not arbitrary java tooling

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256

ImProcessCreate

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OpenAM WebAuthn pre-auth Java deserialization payload to /json/authenticate (CVE-2026-62263) · [LLM] OpenAM/Tomcat Java process spawning a shell — post-deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-62263)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
OpenAM WebAuthn pre-auth Java deserialization payload to /json/authenticate (CVE-2026-62263) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to OpenAM's WebAuthn authentication endpoint carrying a base64-encoded Java serialized object (magic bytes AC ED 00 05 => 'rO0AB'). The vuln's ObjectInputFilter allows the AuthenticatorImpl root but leaves the nested gadget graph unchecked, so the attacker delivers the gadget chain inside a serialized authenticator via an attacker-chosen userHandle — pre-auth. A serialized-object marker on the authenticate endpoint is near-unambiguous exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vuln surface: OpenAM WebAuthn authenticator deserialization reached pre-auth via userHandle on the /json/authenticate endpoint. The 'rO0AB' token is the base64 of the Java serialization magic (0xAC 0xED 0x00 0x05) named implicitly by the deserialization sink; its presence on the authenticate endpoint is exploitation, not normal WebAuthn traffic (which sends base64url userHandle, not serialized graphs). defender_kql/falcon/datadog/cloudwatch left empty: this is server-side web-payload telemetry that lives on a WAF/reverse proxy, not Defender AH, FDR, or AWS. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf8h-gq53-288j • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/org.openidentityplatform.openam/openam-auth-webauthn/CVE-2026-45051/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-6c99-87fr-6q7r • https://github.com/OpenIdentityPlatform/OpenAM/wiki/How-to-Setup-WebAuthn-Authentication-in-OpenAM
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest / red-team probing OpenAM with ysoserial or Nuclei deserialization templates (true positive, confirm authorization)
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys) sending crafted deserialization test payloads to the auth endpoint
  • Legitimate WebAuthn logins — these send base64url userHandle values and will NOT contain the 'rO0AB' serialized marker, so they do not match
  • WAF that base64-encodes and re-logs an entire request in a field that happens to already contain a serialized cookie from a different app
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request from the WAF/proxy log (RequestContext/Message). Confirm the payload after 'rO0AB' is a serialized graph and identify the SourceIP, whether the request got HTTP 200/500, and if it was pre-auth (no valid session). 2) CONTAIN: Block the SourceIP at the WAF, take the exposed OpenAM node out of the LB pool, and confirm the org is on openam-auth-webauthn <=16.1.1 (vulnerable) — upgrade past 16.1.1. 3) HUNT: On the OpenAM host, run UC2 (java spawning shell children) for the same time window; review Tomcat/catalina logs for exceptions during readObject; check for new files, cron/systemd persistence, and outbound connections from the Java process.
// OpenAM WebAuthn deserialization RCE - base64 Java serialized object ('rO0AB' = 0xACED0005) to the authenticate endpoint
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/openam/json/authenticate", "/json/authenticate", "/openam/json/realms", "/json/realms")
| where RequestContext has "rO0AB" or Message has "rO0AB" or RequestURL has "rO0AB" or RequestCookies has "rO0AB"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenAM/Tomcat Java process spawning a shell — post-deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-62263) AIExploitation High
Hunts the OpenAM JVM (java/java.exe under Tomcat/catalina) spawning a command interpreter or download tool — the payload-execution stage after the WebAuthn gadget chain fires during readObject(). An IAM/SSO appliance's Java process spawning cmd/powershell/sh/curl is abnormal and high-fidelity for RCE. Rationale: Grounded in the article's sink (WebAuthn readObject/readResolve executes during readObject() before any assertion check) and the affected package org.openidentityplatform.openam. The parent-context filter (openam/catalina/tomcat/org.openidentityplatform in the JVM cmdline) pins this to the OpenAM appliance rather than any JVM, and pairing it with a shell/downloader child is the classic Java-deser RCE process shape. Cross-platform (java on Linux, java.exe on Windows) since OpenAM commonly runs on Tomcat/Linux. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf8h-gq53-288j • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/org.openidentityplatform.openam/openam-auth-webauthn/CVE-2026-45051/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-6c99-87fr-6q7r
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tomcat startup/shutdown wrappers where catalina.sh/java invokes 'sh -c' during normal service lifecycle
  • OpenAM plugin or scripted auth module that legitimately calls Runtime.exec for a health-check or LDAP helper script
  • Sysadmin running diagnostics under the tomcat/openam service account (whoami, curl to an internal health URL)
  • Monitoring/backup agent shelling out from the JVM for metrics collection
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina.sh start","catalina.sh stop","catalina.sh run","-version","/usr/bin/id -u","/healthcheck","/monitoring/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — decode any base64/encoded command, and check whether it is a known startup script (catalina.sh) or a recon command (whoami, id, curl to attacker host). Correlate the timestamp against UC1 hits (serialized payload to /json/authenticate) on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the OpenAM host, kill the offending child and its descendants, and rotate OpenAM service-account and any credentials the JVM could read (LDAP bind, datastore, secrets). 3) HUNT: Search for webshells under the Tomcat webapps dir, new persistence (cron, systemd, Run keys), outbound C2 from the java process, and lateral auth from the OpenAM host; confirm the fix (openam-auth-webauthn > 16.1.1) is deployed everywhere.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openam","catalina","tomcat","webauthn","org.openidentityplatform")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe","whoami","whoami.exe","python","python3","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java","java.exe","javaw.exe","catalina")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("openam","catalina","tomcat","webauthn","org.openidentityplatform")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","/bash","/sh","/dash","curl","wget","whoami","python","/nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades Go implant C2 beacon to redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com and Hunt.io-named IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections and DNS lookups to the Hades implant's command-and-control infrastructure recovered from the exposed Thai MoF staging server. Fires on the hardcoded C2 domain redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com and the four attacker-controlled IPs linked via shared JA4X TLS fingerprint. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 domain (redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com) embedded in the recovered Hades implant plus the four IPs Hunt.io tied together via shared JA4X TLS certificate fingerprint. Static IOCs = high fidelity. CloudWatch left empty because this is host/network C2 telemetry, not AWS CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately resolving or connecting to the published IOC domain from a sandbox
  • IOC-validation or BAS tooling replaying the indicators against EDR
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the Hong Kong/Malaysia hosts are later reassigned to benign tenants
  • Proxy/NAT egress causing all internal hosts to appear as one SrcIp
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","ti-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host + initiating process (InitiatingProcessSHA256) that reached the IOC; confirm the process image matches a staged Hades build. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the four IPs and redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com at egress/DNS sinkhole, capture memory + the implant binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same InitiatingProcessSHA256 and the five Hades hashes org-wide, review LinPEAS/suo5 execution and Hadoop/Ambari/GlassFish auth logs on the same host.

Hades Go implant payload written or executed (SHA256 match) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any of the five recovered Hades implant SHA256 hashes (Windows + Linux builds) landing on disk or executing. These are the previously undocumented Go implants Hunt.io recovered from the exposed staging directories. Rationale: Directly ships the five Hades SHA256 hashes Hunt.io recovered (62 Windows/Linux builds staged). Hash IOCs are the highest-fidelity signal available and cover both the file-drop and execution moments. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1587.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine copy re-triggering a file-write event on the same hash
  • Malware-analysis or reverse-engineering host intentionally holding the samples
  • Backup/forensic imaging tools re-reading the sample from an evidence share
  • Threat-intel feed auto-download of the sample into a detonation VM
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("sandbox","malware","re-lab","forensic")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit is a live host (not a lab/sandbox); pull FolderPath and the initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, quarantine the binary, snapshot memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 IOCs from UC1 on that host, and sweep for LinPEAS/suo5 artifacts and Hadoop/Ambari/GlassFish access from the same asset.

Customized LinPEAS privilege-escalation enumeration on Linux host AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the LinPEAS enumeration Hermes was instructed to run against a Ministry of Finance host, plus the SUID/SGID discovery it performed. Targets the specific enumeration behaviour (linpeas invocation and find -perm SUID/SGID sweeps) captured in the recovered Hermes call logs. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that Hermes ran a customized LinPEAS against a MoF host; the 'linpeas' string and the SUID/SGID find -perm sweeps are LinPEAS's signature enumeration steps, keeping this tied to the specific tradecraft rather than generic recon. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html
ATT&CKT1082 T1083 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal pentest / red-team running LinPEAS during an engagement
  • Security hardening / CIS-benchmark scripts that legitimately sweep for SUID/SGID binaries
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting file permissions with find -perm
  • Vulnerability scanners (e.g. Lynis) performing SUID enumeration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("lynis","cis-","oscap","tripwire") and AccountName !in~ ("pentest","redteam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host/user is part of an authorized assessment; review the parent process and surrounding command history for staged tooling. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and suspend the account that ran the enumeration. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the LPE exploit attempts (UC4), Hades hashes (UC2), and outbound C2 (UC1); review Hadoop/Ambari/GlassFish auth for adjacent lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "linpeas"
   or (FileName == "find" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-perm -4000","-perm -2000","-perm -u=s","-perm -g=s"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "linpeas"
   or (ActingProcessName == "find" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-perm -4000","-perm -2000","-perm -u=s","-perm -g=s"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Linux local privilege escalation attempt (PwnKit CVE-2021-4034 / Baron Samedit CVE-2021-3156) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts execution shapes of the two Linux LPE exploits whose code was staged in the exposed directories: PwnKit (pkexec invoked with zero arguments) and Baron Samedit (sudoedit with the -s flag). Matches Hermes' stated goal of finding a way to elevate privileges. Rationale: The article states exploit code for CVE-2021-4034 and CVE-2021-3156 was staged and Hermes was tasked to elevate privileges. pkexec-with-no-args (argc=0) is the canonical PwnKit signature and sudoedit -s is the Baron Samedit trigger — both are anomalous vs legitimate use. Sigma omitted because the PwnKit no-argument condition is not expressible as a single Sigma selection. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare legitimate pkexec wrapper scripts that invoke pkexec via a symlink with an empty argv[0] (very uncommon)
  • Automation that calls sudoedit with -s in an edge-case config-management flow
  • Security testing / patch-validation replaying PwnKit or Baron Samedit PoCs
  • Telemetry truncation dropping pkexec arguments, making a legit call look argument-less
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","patch-test") and AccountName !in~ ("pentest","redteam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the pkexec/sudoedit host is patched; check whether the running user gained a root shell immediately after (child process integrity/UID change). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the escalated session, force credential rotation for accounts on the box. 3) Hunt: correlate with LinPEAS enumeration (UC3) on the same host and sweep for Hades payloads (UC2) and suo5 tunnels (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "pkexec" and ProcessCommandLine !contains " ")
   or (FileName =~ "sudoedit" and ProcessCommandLine has "-s")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName =~ "pkexec" and ActingProcessCommandLine !contains " ")
   or (ActingProcessName =~ "sudoedit" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-s")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE ((@process.name:sudoedit AND @process.command_line:*\-s*) OR @process.name:pkexec)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ((ImageFileName=/\/pkexec$/i AND NOT CommandLine=/\s/) OR (ImageFileName=/\/sudoedit$/i AND CommandLine=/-s\b/i))
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="pkexec" AND NOT Processes.process="* *") OR (Processes.process_name="sudoedit" AND Processes.process="*-s*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="pkexec" AND NOT Processes.process="* *") OR (Processes.process_name="sudoedit" AND Processes.process="*-s*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Web/app-server process spawning shell (PHP web shell / suo5 HTTP tunnel) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the PHP web shell Hunt.io says was deployed on a MoF web server and the suo5 HTTP tunneling tool used against the environment, by flagging web/app-server processes (Apache, nginx, php-fpm, GlassFish/Java, IIS) spawning shells or recon binaries, plus any process referencing suo5. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed artifacts: a PHP web shell deployed on a MoF web server and (corroborated by Hunt.io) suo5 HTTP tunnels. Web/app-server parent spawning a shell is the core web-shell command-execution signal for the named Apache/GlassFish/PHP stack; the suo5 keyword adds a tool-specific pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP/CGI apps that shell out (e.g. imagemagick/ffmpeg wrappers, health-check scripts running id/uname)
  • CI/CD or deployment hooks where the web user runs shell commands
  • Monitoring agents invoking curl/wget from under the web-server service account
  • A benign internal tool coincidentally named or pathed with 'suo5'
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("healthcheck","deploy","imagemagick","ffmpeg") and not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","localhost","/health"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the web-server access logs around the same timestamp for the requesting IP and URI (the web-shell endpoint). 2) Contain: pull the offending web file, block the source IP, take the web app offline or into read-only, snapshot the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate other files written by the web-server user, look for suo5 tunnel egress and the Hades/C2 IOCs (UC1/UC2), and review Ambari/GlassFish/Hadoop admin auth from the same server.
let webParents = dynamic(["httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-cgi","php","w3wp.exe","java","tomcat"]);
let shells = dynamic(["sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (webParents) and FileName in~ (shells))
   or ProcessCommandLine has "suo5" or FileName has "suo5"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let webParents = dynamic(["httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-cgi","php","w3wp.exe","java","tomcat"]);
let shells = dynamic(["sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ParentProcessName in~ (webParents) and ActingProcessName in~ (shells))
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has "suo5" or ActingProcessName has "suo5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("43.246.208.207", "103.97.0.57", "118.107.222.232", "202.181.27.115") or RemoteUrl has_any ("redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["43.246.208.207", "103.97.0.57", "118.107.222.232", "202.181.27.115"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-3156", "CVE-2021-4034", "CVE-2017-7269", "CVE-2026-43503", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-3156", "CVE-2021-4034", "CVE-2017-7269", "CVE-2026-43503", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2021-3156", "CVE-2021-4034", "CVE-2017-7269", "CVE-2026-43503", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2021-3156", "CVE-2021-4034", "CVE-2017-7269", "CVE-2026-43503", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-43284", "CVE-2026-43500")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2") or SHA1 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2") or MD5 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2") or SHA1 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2") or MD5 in~ ("0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hackers hijack hotel Wi-Fi DNS to steal Microsoft 365 accounts

BleepingComputer
2026-07-24 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers are changing the DNS settings on Wi-Fi devices at hotels and conference centers to redirect users to fake Microsoft 365 login pages. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566

IPs38.146.28.75 31.57.243.154 104.194.159.150

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Endpoint DNS/connection to hotel-WiFi M365 phishing infrastructure (ms365-* domains + IPs) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Entra ID sign-in from hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack campaign infrastructure IPs · [LLM] Malicious WPAD/PAC proxy auto-config fetch on untrusted network · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Endpoint DNS/connection to hotel-WiFi M365 phishing infrastructure (ms365-* domains + IPs) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the four fake Microsoft 365 login domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com) and three IPs used by the ReliaQuest-reported hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack campaign. Because the gateway forges plaintext DNS, endpoints land on attacker infrastructure while believing they reached login.microsoftonline.com — a direct hit on any of these indicators is a travelling-employee compromise signal. Rationale: Uses the four attacker-registered phishing FQDNs (corroborated across ReliaQuest, BleepingComputer, SecurityAffairs, GBHackers) plus the three campaign IPs from the article. Any resolution/connection is a hard IOC hit with near-zero legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196017/security/hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-credentials.html • https://gbhackers.com/hotel-wi-fi-dns-poisoning-attacks/
ATT&CKT1557 T1566.002 T1584.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst sandboxing/browsing the phishing domain for triage
  • Threat-intel platform or URL-detonation appliance actively probing the IOC
  • Typosquat-monitoring service that crawls newly-registered Microsoft-lookalike domains
  • DNS sinkhole/allowlist tooling that resolves the domain to log it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") // exclude Defender detonation/telemetry probes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the user/device that resolved or connected; confirm the source is a corporate endpoint (not a sandbox/TI probe) and whether the host was recently on hotel/conference guest Wi-Fi. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke all Entra refresh tokens for the affected user, force password reset + re-registration of MFA, and isolate the endpoint if a POST to the domain occurred. 3) HUNT: Pivot to SigninLogs for that UPN from the campaign IPs and any device-code sign-ins, and search other org hosts for the same four domains/three IPs to scope travelling-employee exposure.
let BadDomains = dynamic(["m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com"]);
let BadIPs = dynamic(["38.146.28.75","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (BadDomains) or RemoteIP in (BadIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadDomains = dynamic(["m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com"]);
let BadIPs = dynamic(["38.146.28.75","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (BadDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=ClientIP, Host=Computer, Indicator=Name, Kind="dns"),
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (BadIPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (BadDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Host=SourceHostName, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationIP), Kind="firewall")
)

id: 8f2c1a44-7e30-4b21-9b8c-2f9d0a6e1c77
description: Detects DNS resolution of the fake Microsoft 365 login domains used in the ReliaQuest hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack campaign.

Entra ID sign-in from hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack campaign infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects successful or attempted Microsoft 365 sign-ins originating from the three IPs tied to the hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack campaign. Because the actor abuses the device-code flow, a legitimate OAuth token is issued to the attacker's client — so a sign-in (interactive or the non-interactive polling leg) from this infrastructure is post-phish account takeover, MFA notwithstanding. Rationale: Anchors on the three campaign IPs and correlates both the interactive and non-interactive (device-code polling) sign-in legs, matching ReliaQuest's description of an OAuth token issued to the attacker's client without credential theft. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/ • https://github.com/reprise99/Sentinel-Queries/blob/main/Azure%20Active%20Directory/Identity-DeviceCodePhishing.kql
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN/egress that happens to share an ASN block with the flagged IP (verify exact /32)
  • Threat-intel enrichment service authenticating from a research IP that overlaps
  • Recycled cloud IP reassigned to a benign tenant after the campaign window
  • Analyst reproducing the device-code flow during a purple-team exercise
Suppression filter
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com" or ResultType == 0 // keep successful auths; refine to your break-glass/service accounts
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each hit confirm ResultType (0 = success) and whether ClientAppUsed/IsInteractive indicate the device-code flow; check the resource accessed (Graph, Exchange, SharePoint). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), disable the account pending reset, and block the three IPs at Conditional Access; disable Device Code auth flow via CA if not required. 3) HUNT: Enumerate mailbox rules, Graph app consents, and OAuth grants created by the account after the sign-in; scope any other UPNs seen from the same IPs.
let BadIPs = dynamic(["38.146.28.75","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in (BadIPs)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, ErrorCode, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadIPs = dynamic(["38.146.28.75","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress in (BadIPs) | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ResultType, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, UserAgent, Location),
  (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress in (BadIPs) | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ResultType, ClientAppUsed)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: M365 Sign-in From Hotel Wi-Fi DNS-Hijack Campaign IP
id: b1d47f2e-9a06-4c58-8d11-6c3ab7e4f902
description: Detects Entra ID sign-ins sourced from the three IPs attributed to the hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack / device-code phishing campaign.
references:

  - https://github.com/reprise99/Sentinel-Queries/blob/main/Azure%20Active%20Directory/Identity-DeviceCodePhishing.kql
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:

  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1621
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    IpAddress:
      - '38.146.28.75'
      - '31.57.243.154'
      - '104.194.159.150'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" (@network.client.ip:38.146.28.75 OR @network.client.ip:31.57.243.154 OR @network.client.ip:104.194.159.150)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.src IN ("38.146.28.75","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150") by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.src IN ("38.146.28.75","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150") by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Malicious WPAD/PAC proxy auto-config fetch on untrusted network AICommand & Control Low
Hunts endpoints retrieving a wpad.dat or .pac proxy-config file over the public internet, matching the campaign's observed WPAD abuse where the hijacked gateway answers Windows' automatic WPAD lookup with a malicious PAC file to route app/browser traffic through an attacker proxy. On a corporate network WPAD stays intranet-scoped, so a public-facing PAC retrieval is anomalous. Rationale: Targets the article's WPAD-abuse leg (malicious PAC served in response to Windows' automatic WPAD lookup) via the wpad.dat/.pac retrieval string and a public-network scope; kept hunting/Low because ReliaQuest could not confirm the WPAD attacks succeeded. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-dns-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1557 T1090.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise WPAD/PAC hosted on an internet-facing corporate URL (allowlist that host)
  • SaaS/VPN client legitimately publishing a .pac file for split-tunnel config
  • Roaming laptop on a partner network with its own valid WPAD server
  • Web dev/test traffic requesting files ending in .pac unrelated to proxy config
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("wpad.corp.", "pac.corp.")) // exclude sanctioned corporate WPAD/PAC hosts — tune to your domain
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the device was on untrusted (hotel/conference) Wi-Fi and inspect the fetched PAC content and the AutoConfigURL registry value (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings\AutoConfigURL) for an attacker host. 2) CONTAIN: Clear the malicious proxy/AutoConfigURL, disable WPAD on the endpoint, and force full-tunnel VPN; revoke M365 tokens if the proxy could have intercepted auth. 3) HUNT: Look for the four phishing domains and three campaign IPs from that host, and any Entra sign-ins for its user from the campaign IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "wpad.dat" or RemoteUrl endswith ".pac"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has "wpad.dat" or RequestURL endswith ".pac"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WPAD/PAC Proxy Auto-Config Retrieval
id: c73a5e19-2b84-4d6f-a0e2-8f1c4b9d7e30
description: Detects retrieval of a wpad.dat or .pac proxy auto-configuration file, abused by the hotel Wi-Fi DNS-hijack campaign to route traffic through an attacker proxy.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-dns-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1557
  - attack.t1090.001
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'wpad.dat'
      - '.pac'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*wpad* OR *WPAD*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^wpad\./i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*wpad.dat*" OR Web.url="*.pac") Web.dest_category!="internal" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*wpad.dat*" OR Web.url="*.pac") Web.dest_category!="internal" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

CloudAppEvents

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent

| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
